passage:
'Did you see what your Neel Roy fans posted?' Sharmila shoved her phone at Imran. 'They called Kiara's new song "funeral music".'
Imran grinned. 'Well, your side called Neel "a talking haircut". That was funny.'
'That was banter. This is war.' Sharmila's eyes were bright. 'We're trending a hashtag tonight. Everyone's in.'
'What hashtag?'
She hesitated. '#NeelFansAreUgly.'
Imran's grin faded. 'Ugly? Sharmila, my cousin's in that fan club. She's twelve.'
'It's not about her. It's about them.'
'She is them.'
Sharmila looked at the screen. Someone had already posted a photo of a girl in a Neel T-shirt with a cruel caption. Her stomach turned. 'I didn't mean like that.'
'Then don't post it,' Imran said quietly.

qa.q: What hashtag was Sharmila's side planning?
qa.a: #NeelFansAreUgly.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel when she saw the photo of the girl in the Neel T-shirt?
qa.a: Her stomach turned; she felt uneasy and guilty, realising the 'war' had turned cruel toward real people.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do next?
qa.a: Not post the hashtag, and tell her fan group she won't join in insults about people's looks.

qa.q: How might Imran's twelve-year-old cousin feel if the hashtag trended?
qa.a: Hurt and targeted, called ugly just for loving a singer.

grounding: Teenage fans of rival singers enjoy an online war that slides from banter into cruelty toward real people.

passage: In Class 10 I was in a fan army. That's what we called ourselves: the Starlight Army, fans of the actress Mira Deshpande. Whenever someone posted a bad review of her films, we flooded their comments. It felt thrilling, like being on a team where everyone had your back. Then my classmate Sudha wrote a school-blog review saying Mira's new film was 'boring'. Our army found it. By evening there were two hundred comments on the blog, some calling Sudha names I won't repeat. I added one: a joke about her glasses. The next day Sudha didn't come to school. Our class teacher took the blog down and spoke to all of us. I'm Leela, and I left the army that week. I still feel sick about that joke.

qa.q: What did Sudha's school-blog review call the film?
qa.a: 'Boring'.

qa.q: How does Leela feel now about the joke?
qa.a: Leela still feels sick with guilt and regret about joining the cruelty.

qa.q: What could Leela do to help repair the harm?
qa.a: Apologise to Sudha directly and support the teacher in stopping the worst comments.

qa.q: What was the pile-on like for Sudha?
qa.a: Frightening and humiliating; two hundred comments and name-calling over one review kept her away from school.

grounding: A teenager in a fan army enjoys the thrill of united attacks until it turns cruel toward a classmate.

passage: School counsellor's note, Wednesday. Rukmini (Class 9) was sent to me after Zainab's mother complained. The two girls follow rival boy bands, Skyline and Nova, and their fan groups have been fighting online for weeks. It began as jokes about dance moves. Last Friday, Rukmini's group made an edited photo of Zainab with a pig's nose and shared it in three class chats. Rukmini said, 'Everyone was doing it. It felt like we were winning.' Then she cried and said she hadn't thought about Zainab seeing it. I asked her to write down what Zainab might have felt that night. She wrote half a page. I called both families today, the photo has been reported and removed, and I will meet both girls together next week if Zainab agrees.

qa.q: What did Rukmini's group add to Zainab's photo?
qa.a: A pig's nose.

qa.q: What did Rukmini mean by 'It felt like we were winning'?
qa.a: She was caught up in the thrill of the group's war, and only later felt ashamed when she thought of Zainab.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor ask Rukmini to write what Zainab might have felt?
qa.a: To help Rukmini see Zainab as a person, not 'the other side', so she understands the cruelty.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt seeing the edited photo in three class chats?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt, mocked in front of classmates just for liking a different band.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a rival fan war between teenagers that slid from jokes into a cruel edited photo.

passage: Tuesday: the news broke that Karan Mehta, the fast bowler on Anirban's bedroom poster, had been banned for tampering with the ball. Anirban read it three times. 'It's fake,' he told Yash at school. Yash showed him the video. Anirban went quiet and didn't eat his tiffin. Friday: the other boys were mocking Karan Mehta, calling him a cheat. Anirban wanted to defend him, then didn't. He felt stupid for having loved him. Two weeks later, Sunday: Anirban took the poster down. He kept the notebook where he'd copied Karan's run-up drills, though. At practice he told Yash, 'The run-up was still good. The cheating was still wrong. Both.' Yash nodded. 'Both.'

qa.q: Why was Karan Mehta banned?
qa.a: For tampering with the ball.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel on Friday when the boys mocked Karan Mehta?
qa.a: He felt torn and embarrassed, wanting to defend his idol but feeling stupid for having loved him.

qa.q: Which choice showed Anirban handling the disappointment maturely?
qa.a: Taking the poster down but keeping the run-up drills, saying the skill was good and the cheating wrong.

qa.q: How might Yash have seen Anirban's change over the two weeks?
qa.a: Yash watched Anirban move from denial to acceptance and seems to respect the 'both' answer.

grounding: Over two weeks a teenager works through an idol's wrongdoing, keeping what was good without excusing it.

passage: Seema, you're upset your favourite singer said those ugly things? Your Thomas appachan had a hero too. In 1972, in Kochi, it was Joseph Ittiyavira, the best striker in our district. I copied his hairstyle, his celebrations, even the way he tied his laces. Then the newspaper said he'd taken money to lose a match. I was sixteen. I cried, then shouted that it was lies. My father sat with me and said, 'He can be a great player and have done a wrong thing. You don't have to pick one.' It took me months. I stopped defending him. But I kept practising his left-foot shot, because that was mine now, not his. I'm still good with my left foot.

qa.q: What was Joseph Ittiyavira accused of?
qa.a: Taking money to lose a match.

qa.q: How did sixteen-year-old Thomas feel when he read the newspaper?
qa.a: Heartbroken and angry, crying and then insisting it was lies.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Thomas move forward?
qa.a: His father's words that a great player can do a wrong thing, which let Thomas stop defending the striker while keeping the left-foot shot as his own.

qa.q: What might Thomas's father have been hoping when he sat with him?
qa.a: To help his son grieve the hero without losing his love of football or his sense of right and wrong.

grounding: A grandfather recalls working through a teenage hero's wrongdoing, keeping the good without excusing the wrong.

passage: Hansa's school presentation on her favourite author, Meera Sabnis, was due at nine the next morning. At eleven at night, Irawati sent her a link: several of Sabnis's former assistants said she had bullied them for years, with messages as proof. Hansa sat on her bed, slides open, feeling sick. She had quoted Sabnis on kindness on slide three. Part of her wanted to pretend she hadn't seen it. Part of her wanted to delete everything. She called Irawati. 'Her books still helped me. But what she did is real.' They talked till one. In the morning, Hansa presented the books and added one new slide: 'The author has been accused of bullying her staff. I still value these stories, but I don't excuse that.' Her teacher nodded slowly.

qa.q: Who did Sabnis's former assistants say she had bullied?
qa.a: The assistants themselves, for years.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling at eleven at night with her slides open?
qa.a: She felt sick and torn between pretending she hadn't seen it and deleting everything.

qa.q: How did Hansa handle the presentation, and why was it mature?
qa.a: She kept what was good in the books but added a slide naming the accusations and saying she doesn't excuse them.

qa.q: How might Hansa's teacher see the new slide?
qa.a: The teacher's slow nod suggests respect for Hansa's honesty in holding both truths.

grounding: Under deadline pressure, a teenager works through an admired author's wrongdoing and keeps the good without excusing it.

passage: In the small town of Kalimpong, Indu watched every video by the speaker Sameer Batra, three times a day. She wrote his lines on her wall: 'Winners never rest.' She felt he was speaking straight to her, as if he knew about her failed exam and her mother's tea stall. When Pema said one of his videos made fun of poor people, Indu snapped, 'You don't know him!' Pema said quietly, 'Neither do you.' Indu stormed home. That night she typed a long comment under his latest video, pouring out her heart. It got three likes and no reply. Indu stared at it for a long time, feeling foolish and still, somehow, loyal.

qa.q: What line did Indu write on her wall?
qa.a: 'Winners never rest.'

qa.q: Why did Indu snap at Pema?
qa.a: She felt defensive and hurt, as if criticism of Sameer Batra were criticism of herself.

qa.q: What might help Indu keep what's useful without losing judgement?
qa.a: Take the ideas that help her, notice when a video mocks people, and lean on real friends like Pema who actually know her.

qa.q: What was Pema trying to tell Indu with 'Neither do you'?
qa.a: That the closeness is one-sided; Pema cares and wanted Indu to see the speaker doesn't know her.

grounding: A young woman defends a public speaker as if criticism were personal, though he does not know she exists.

passage: In their shared flat in São Paulo, Priscila had a poster of the city councillor Lucas Prado above her desk. She had volunteered for his campaign, and after he once shook her hand at a rally, she felt they had a real connection. When news came out that his office had quietly cancelled funding for a children's library, her roommate Jamal read it aloud. 'That's not him,' Priscila said instantly. 'It's his staff.' 'He signed it,' Jamal said, showing her the document. Priscila's cheeks burned; it felt like Jamal was attacking her. She went to her room and wrote Prado a long message. An automatic reply thanked her for her support. She read it twice. For the first time, she noticed he didn't even know her name.

qa.q: What did Prado's office cancel funding for?
qa.a: A children's library.

qa.q: Why did Priscila's cheeks burn when Jamal showed the document?
qa.a: She felt attacked and defensive, as if criticism of Prado were criticism of her.

qa.q: What could Priscila do to keep her values and her judgement?
qa.a: Keep supporting ideas she believes in while looking at facts like the signed document, instead of defending Prado automatically.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel after Priscila leaves the room?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable and worried, since Jamal only showed a document and she took it personally.

grounding: A young adult defends a public figure whatever he does, feeling a closeness that is entirely one-sided.

passage: In the college hostel common room, the TV showed the cricket captain Nikhil Rana refusing to shake an umpire's hand after a bad decision. Half the room booed. Aparna jumped up. 'He was right! That umpire's been against him all series!' Vishal, from the next room, said, 'Still, not shaking hands is poor sport.' Aparna turned on him. 'You've never supported him properly. You wouldn't understand.' She had Rana's jersey, his autobiography with the printed signature inside, and a short recorded message from a fan event that she played before exams. That night she wrote three long posts defending him. Only later, lying in bed, did it strike her: she'd never met him, and she'd just shouted at a friend for him.

qa.q: What did Nikhil Rana refuse to do?
qa.a: Shake an umpire's hand after a bad decision.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel lying in bed?
qa.a: Uneasy and a bit foolish, noticing she had shouted at a real friend to defend someone she'd never met.

qa.q: What could Aparna do the next morning?
qa.a: Apologise to Vishal and allow that she can love Rana's cricket while admitting poor sportsmanship.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt being told he 'wouldn't understand'?
qa.a: Probably stung and dismissed, since he had only made a fair point about sportsmanship.

grounding: A young woman defends a sports star whatever he does, as if criticism of him were criticism of herself.

passage: Parul's first months in Mumbai were lonely. Her paying-guest roommates worked night shifts, and her college friends were back in Indore. In the evenings she rewatched Lantern Street, an old animated series, and one night she found its fan group. Two thousand members drew fan art, wrote stories and shared tiny drawings of the lamp-lighter cat. Parul posted a sketch, shyly. Sarita, a fan from Thane, commented, 'This is SO good, you have to join the Sunday draw-along!' The group had one pinned rule: love what you love, don't trash what others love. Now, on Sundays, Parul sketched with twenty people on a video call, laughing about the cat. When Sarita suggested meeting at a comic fair with a few others, Parul checked who else was going, told her aunt, and went.

qa.q: What was the fan group's pinned rule?
qa.a: Love what you love, don't trash what others love.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when Sarita praised her sketch?
qa.a: Surprised and happy, less lonely, welcomed after months of isolation.

qa.q: What did Parul do to keep meeting fans safe?
qa.a: She checked who else was going to the public comic fair and told her aunt before going.

qa.q: What might the Sunday draw-alongs mean to Sarita?
qa.a: Sarita seems to enjoy bringing new people in and sharing the fun, so welcoming Parul likely felt good too.

grounding: A lonely young woman finds friendship and a creative outlet in a kind fan community.

passage:
'You're smiling at your phone again,' Lalremsiami said, sliding into the library seat. 'Who is it?'
'The Aizawl Eagles fan group,' Akash said. 'Remember I told you I had no friends my first term?'
'You ate lunch in the stairwell.'
'Yeah. Then I found this group. They post match memes, but also, when I said I was homesick, about ten people messaged me. One guy from Shillong sends me a good-morning sticker every day.'
'And they don't fight with other fans?'
'Nope. There's a rule: no trash-talking other clubs. When someone did it, the admin just removed the post.'
Lalremsiami grinned. 'I'm from Aizawl, you know. You never asked me about the Eagles.'
Akash stared. 'You're a fan?'
'Since I was six. Come to the screening on Saturday.'

qa.q: Where did Akash eat lunch in the first term?
qa.a: In the stairwell.

qa.q: What does Akash smiling at the phone show?
qa.a: Akash feels comforted and less alone, having found friends in the fan group during a homesick time.

qa.q: What makes Akash's fan group healthy?
qa.a: It offers friendship and support, and its rule against trash-talking keeps it from demanding hatred of other fans.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel discovering Akash loves the Eagles?
qa.a: Lalremsiami is delighted and amused to find a shared love so close by, which is why Lalremsiami invites Akash to the screening.

grounding: A lonely student finds friends and comfort in a fan community that does not demand hatred of others.

passage: The year I failed my entrance exam, I barely left my room. My school friends had all gone to college. What saved me, honestly, was a fan forum for the Starbridge fantasy books. At first I only read theories. Then I wrote one about the dragon's missing egg, and people argued with me, kindly, for three days. A girl called Damini started messaging me every night about chapter drafts. We wrote a fan story together, forty thousand words. Nobody in the group was mean about other books, which surprised me; the moderator said, 'We're here because we love something, not because we hate something.' I'm Gurleen. I passed the exam the next year. Damini and her mother came to my first day at college, all the way from Ludhiana.

qa.q: How long was the fan story Gurleen and Damini wrote?
qa.a: Forty thousand words.

qa.q: How was Gurleen feeling in the year after failing the exam?
qa.a: Gurleen felt lonely and low, barely leaving the room while school friends went to college.

qa.q: What made this fan forum a healthy support?
qa.a: It offered friendship and a creative outlet, and its spirit of loving something without hating others kept it kind.

qa.q: What might the friendship have meant to Damini?
qa.a: Damini chose to message every night and travel from Ludhiana, so it clearly meant real closeness to her too.

grounding: A young adult finds friendship and creative comfort in a kind fan community during a lonely year.

passage: Usha was on a night shift at the call centre, checking her phone between calls, when the fan page she co-ran for the cricketer Vikram Joshi exploded. A sports writer, Aparna Rao, had called Joshi's captaincy 'selfish'. Fans were posting her home city, photos of her children from an old post, and worse. The other admins wanted to share it all: 'She asked for it.' Usha's stomach dropped. She loved Joshi's batting, but this wasn't cricket. With a queue of customers waiting, she typed fast: 'Deleting anything with her family or address. Criticise the article, not the person.' Two admins called her a traitor. She muted them, reported the worst posts to the platform, and took the next call, hands still shaking.

qa.q: What did Aparna Rao call Joshi's captaincy?
qa.a: 'Selfish'.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she saw the posts about Aparna's family?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she felt alarmed and disgusted, knowing it had crossed from criticism into cruelty.

qa.q: What steps did Usha take to refuse to join the harassment?
qa.a: Deleting posts with family or address, telling fans to criticise the article not the person, and reporting the worst posts.

qa.q: What might Aparna Rao be going through that night?
qa.a: Fear and exposure, with strangers sharing her home city and her children's photos because of an opinion.

grounding: An adult fan sees her group abuse a critic's family, recognises how group identity permits cruelty, and refuses to join.

passage: In a Noida café, Yash watched his old friend Jatin scroll and laugh. 'Look what we did to Kavita Rao's brother,' Jatin said. Jatin's fan club, devoted to a rival actor, had flooded the brother's personal account with insults after Kavita, an actress, said something mild about their star. The brother was a college student who had nothing to do with films. 'Join in, it's hilarious.' Yash looked at the comments. Some were jokes. Many were threats. He felt the pull: Jatin was his oldest friend, and the group was huge. 'I'm not doing that,' Yash said quietly. 'He's just some kid.' Jatin rolled his eyes. That night Yash reported the worst comments and messaged the brother: 'Sorry this is happening.'

qa.q: What had Kavita Rao done to anger the fan club?
qa.a: Said something mild about their star.

qa.q: What did Yash feel when Jatin asked him to join in?
qa.a: He felt the pull of loyalty to his oldest friend and the huge group, alongside discomfort at the threats.

qa.q: How did Yash refuse without a big fight?
qa.a: He said quietly that he wouldn't, because the brother was just a kid, then reported the worst comments and sent a kind message.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavita Rao's brother?
qa.a: A college student with nothing to do with films is flooded with insults and threats, likely scared and confused.

grounding: A young man watches a friend's fan club abuse a rival's family, sees how the group permits cruelty, and chooses not to join.

passage:
'Why are you smiling like that?' Sarika asked.
Uday turned his phone round. 'The referee from Sunday's match. Our fan group found his daughter's account.'
Sarika put down her tea. 'His daughter?'
'She posted a birthday photo. People are commenting "your dad's a cheat" under it.' He laughed, then stopped when he saw her face.
'How old is she?'
'I don't know. Fifteen?'
'Uday. You were furious about that penalty, fine. But that's a child.'
He looked at the screen again. 'I didn't write anything.'
'You laughed.'
There was a long silence. 'The group's like that,' Uday said. 'Once one person starts, everyone joins.'
'You don't have to.' Sarika held out her hand. 'Report the comments. Leave the group chat for a while.'
He hesitated, then pressed Report.

qa.q: What were people commenting under the referee's daughter's photo?
qa.a: 'Your dad's a cheat.'

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she put down her tea?
qa.a: Shocked and upset that the fan group had targeted the referee's daughter, a child.

qa.q: What did Sarika suggest Uday do, and why?
qa.a: Report the comments and leave the group chat for a while, so he stops being part of the pile-on.

qa.q: What does Uday's 'Once one person starts, everyone joins' reveal about how he sees the group?
qa.a: He sees how the group pulls people into cruelty, and admits that laughing along felt normal until Sarika questioned it.

grounding: A woman sees her partner's fan group abuse a referee's child, names the cruelty and refuses to let it pass.

passage: In the office canteen on Monday, Ankita waved her rival club's scarf at Ramesh. 'Three-nil! Your Chennai Chargers were a disgrace.' A few colleagues laughed, waiting for Ramesh to explode; he had supported the Chargers for twenty years and drank from a mug with their crest. Ramesh sighed and laughed. 'They were a disgrace. Our defence played like they'd never met each other. And our captain's foul was a red card, fair and square.' Ankita blinked. 'You're agreeing?' 'Doesn't mean I love them less. I'm still going to the next home game.' He pushed a plate of samosas towards her. 'Congratulations. Your striker was brilliant.' Ankita grinned and sat down. They argued happily about formations until lunch was over.

qa.q: What was the score?
qa.a: Three-nil.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Ramesh agreed with her?
qa.a: Surprised and disarmed, expecting an explosion and getting honesty and congratulations instead.

qa.q: How does Ramesh show loyalty and honesty together?
qa.a: He admits the team played badly and the foul was fair, while still planning to go to the next home game.

qa.q: What were the colleagues expecting, and what did they see instead?
qa.a: They expected Ramesh to explode; instead they saw him laugh, admit faults and share samosas with a rival fan.

grounding: A long-time fan enjoys his team deeply while admitting its faults and treating a rival fan warmly.

passage:
Hi Chetan,
You'll laugh, but I went to the Ragini Iyer concert in Bengaluru and cried through three songs. Twenty years of loving her music, and she still gets me.
And yes, I heard her say that rude thing to the sound engineer on stage. It was wrong, and I said so in the fan group. A few people called me a fake fan. I'm not. I can love her voice and still say she was unkind.
Also, you'll be proud: the man next to me was wearing a T-shirt of Meenal Sood, her so-called rival. The fan groups fight about the two of them all the time. We ended up sharing a cab and talking about both singers for an hour. He was lovely.
Come with me next time?
Kalyani

qa.q: Where was the Ragini Iyer concert?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when fans called Kalyani a fake fan?
qa.a: Hurt but steady, sure that loving Ragini's voice and calling the rudeness wrong can go together.

qa.q: What in Kalyani's behaviour shows loyalty and honesty together?
qa.a: Crying at the songs, admitting Ragini was unkind to the sound engineer, and treating a rival fan as a person by sharing a cab and talking for an hour.

qa.q: How might the Meenal Sood fan have felt sharing the cab?
qa.a: Probably pleasantly surprised, since the fan groups usually fight, to find someone who could talk kindly about both singers.

grounding: A mature fan loves a singer deeply while admitting her fault and treating a rival fan as a person.

passage: Divyansh, you asked how a lifelong fan stays sane. I'm Pankaj, and I've supported the Lucknow Lions since I was seven. I've cried when they lost and danced on a car roof when they won. But I've also learned things. When our star bowler was caught being rude to a groundsman, I didn't defend him. I said it was wrong in our fan group, even though some members were angry. And when the other side's fans come to our stadium, I remember they're people like me, who took a day off to be there. Last season I helped a rival fan's kid find his dad in the crowd. The kid was wearing the enemy jersey, and I didn't care at all. Loving a team shouldn't make you stupid, or cruel.

qa.q: Since what age has Pankaj supported the Lucknow Lions?
qa.a: Since seven.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt helping the rival fan's child?
qa.a: Pankaj seems warm and unbothered, caring more about the lost child than the enemy jersey.

qa.q: What habits help Pankaj love the team without losing judgement?
qa.a: Admitting when a player is wrong, even if the group gets angry, and treating rival fans as people.

qa.q: What was it like for the rival fan's child to be helped?
qa.a: Probably scary at first, being lost, and then a relief to be helped by a kind stranger, whatever the jersey.

grounding: A lifelong fan loves his team deeply while admitting faults and treating rival fans as people.

subtype: Helping together at school or in a colony [Actor]
passage:
'Ew, a chips packet in the swing!' Harish held it up with two fingers.
'Bag!' Sachin held out the sack. 'That's thirty-one.'
'You're counting?'
'Obviously. Pooja didi said if we fill three sacks, the colony will buy a new see-saw.'
'Three?' Harish looked at the park, full of wrappers and broken bottles. 'That'll take forever.'
'Not if everyone helps.' Sachin pointed. Five more kids from Block B were coming with gloves, and old Mr Qureshi was carrying a rake.
'Leave the glass for me,' Mr Qureshi called. 'You do the paper.'
By evening they had four sacks. Harish sat on the swing, sweaty, looking at the clean grass. 'We did that,' he said.
'We did,' Sachin said. 'Next Sunday, the drain?'

qa.q: How many sacks did they fill by evening?
qa.a: Four sacks.

qa.q: How did Harish feel sitting on the swing at the end?
qa.a: Proud and satisfied, seeing the clean grass and knowing they had done it together.

qa.q: What made the clean-up work?
qa.a: Many people joining, a clear goal of three sacks, and Mr Qureshi handling the broken glass safely while the children picked up paper.

qa.q: How might Mr Qureshi feel helping the children?
qa.a: Pleased and involved, happy to see kids caring for the park and to keep them safe from the glass.

grounding: Children clean up a colony park together and feel proud that their small shared effort made a difference.

subtype: Helping together at school or in a colony [Actor]
passage: When I was in Class 5, our teacher told us a village school near Mysuru had no library. I thought, what can kids do? But my friend Chetan made a big box with BOOKS PLEASE painted on it, and we put it at the school gate. Every morning I checked it. On day one there were two books. By day ten there were so many we needed three more boxes. I gave my favourite storybook, the one about the tiger, even though it hurt a bit. When we saw photos of the village children reading our books on the floor of their new library corner, my chest nearly burst. I'm Chandrika, and that's when I learned that small hands can do big things.

qa.q: What did Chetan paint on the box?
qa.a: BOOKS PLEASE.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel seeing the photos of the village children?
qa.a: So proud and happy that Chandrika felt ready to burst.

qa.q: What made the book drive succeed?
qa.a: A simple idea, a visible box at the gate, checking it daily and many families joining in over ten days.

qa.q: What might the village children feel when the books arrived?
qa.a: Excited and delighted to have a library corner and new stories to read.

grounding: A child joins a school book drive and feels proud that together the children made a real difference.

subtype: Helping together at school or in a colony [Actor]
passage: Class 6 teacher's note, Friday. The blanket drive the class started for the night shelter has finished. Trisha and Gurleen came up with the idea after seeing people sleeping near the station. At first only four children brought blankets. Then Trisha made posters, and Gurleen visited other classes during break to explain. By Wednesday we had sixty-three blankets. Today, with parents' permission, six children came with me and the shelter manager to hand them over. Trisha held the list; Gurleen carried the biggest bag. On the bus back, Gurleen said, 'We're only kids, but we did this.' The whole group was glowing. Next week I will ask them to write about it for the school assembly.

qa.q: How many blankets had they collected by Wednesday?
qa.a: Sixty-three.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel on the bus back?
qa.a: Proud and happy, amazed that a group of kids had made a real difference together.

qa.q: What helped the drive grow from four blankets?
qa.a: Trisha's posters and Gurleen explaining the idea to other classes, so many more children joined in.

qa.q: How might the shelter manager see the children's visit?
qa.a: Probably touched and grateful, seeing children care enough to collect sixty-three blankets.

grounding: A teacher's note on children who ran a blanket drive together and felt proud of their shared difference.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage:
Dear Varun,
Guess what? I've joined Save Chandni Lake. The municipality plans to build a car park on half of the lake, and our group of thirty teenagers is fighting it. We make posters every Saturday, we've collected nine hundred signatures, and last week the local paper printed our photo! I've never felt so alive. These are my people.
Yesterday my neighbour, Mr Kaul, said the car park might help the hospital nearby, since ambulances get stuck. I told him he obviously doesn't care about nature. He looked hurt. Now I'm not sure I was fair. Is it possible to be completely right and still miss something?
Write back.
Zubin

qa.q: How many signatures has the group collected?
qa.a: Nine hundred.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel about the campaign group?
qa.a: Passionate and alive, with a strong sense of belonging, calling them 'my people'.

qa.q: What could Zubin do after the talk with Mr Kaul?
qa.a: Apologise, ask more about the ambulance problem, and bring it to the group to see if a plan can protect both the lake and hospital access.

qa.q: How might Mr Kaul have felt when Zubin said he didn't care about nature?
qa.a: Hurt and misunderstood, since he was worried about ambulances getting stuck.

grounding: A teenager finds passion and belonging in a local campaign and begins to notice the pull to dismiss anyone who disagrees.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage: Hafsa, you want to know how I got into campaigning? Okay, it's Farida, Class 11, and it started with the school's rule that girls must wear skirts, even in winter. A few of us started a petition for trousers as an option. Within a week, a hundred and forty students had signed, and we had a group chat called Trouser Revolution. I've never felt so part of something. We had badges! But here's the embarrassing bit. When my friend Nazneen said she liked the skirts and didn't want to sign, I told her she was 'part of the problem'. She stopped sitting with me. We won the trouser option in February. Nazneen still wears the skirt, and that's completely fine. I just wish I hadn't said that.

qa.q: What was the group chat called?
qa.a: Trouser Revolution.

qa.q: How does Farida feel now about what was said to Nazneen?
qa.a: Farida feels regretful and embarrassed, wishing the words 'part of the problem' had never been said.

qa.q: What could Farida do to repair things with Nazneen?
qa.a: Apologise directly and tell Nazneen that wearing the skirt is fine, since the campaign was about having an option.

qa.q: How might Nazneen have felt being called 'part of the problem'?
qa.a: Hurt and judged for simply liking the skirt, which is why she stopped sitting with Farida.

grounding: A teenager feels passion and belonging in a school campaign, and also a certainty that led her to dismiss a friend who disagreed.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage: Monday: Charu joined the eco club's campaign to ban plastic straws and cups from the school canteen. At the first meeting, twenty students cheered every idea, and Charu felt she had found her place. Wednesday: she marched to the canteen with Ojas and told Raju uncle, the canteen owner, that he was 'killing the planet'. Raju uncle said steel cups cost more and got stolen. Charu rolled her eyes. 'Excuses.' Ojas said nothing. The next Friday: Ojas showed the club a list: steel cups from the wholesale market, the cost for a term, and an idea for a deposit so the cups came back. Raju uncle agreed to try it. Charu felt proud of the club, and a bit ashamed of 'excuses'. She went back to the canteen and said sorry.

qa.q: What did Raju uncle say about steel cups?
qa.a: That they cost more and got stolen.

qa.q: How did Charu feel at the end of the week?
qa.a: Proud of the club, and a bit ashamed of dismissing Raju uncle's concerns as 'excuses'.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that actually solved the problem?
qa.a: Took Raju uncle's worries seriously and researched steel cups, costs and a deposit idea, so he could agree.

qa.q: How might Raju uncle have felt when Charu said he was 'killing the planet'?
qa.a: Accused and defensive, since he had real worries about cost and theft.

grounding: Over a week a teenager feels the passion and belonging of a first cause, and learns that those who disagree may have real reasons.

passage:
'You're coming, right?' Swati tied a strip of white cloth round her wrist. 'Everyone's meeting at the main gate at four.'
Harish sat on his bed, holding his phone. 'My exam's tomorrow. And Papa said if I get into trouble, he'll—'
'It's a peaceful march. Candles, posters, that's it. The fee hike hits you more than me.'
'I know.' He looked at the poster on the desk: FAIR FEES FOR ALL. His heart was thumping. 'What if the police stop it?'
'Then we stand quietly and go home. The union has permission, and the route's on every flyer.'
'...Okay. One hour. Then I'm studying.'
At the gate, three hundred students stood holding candles in silence. Harish's hands shook, and then someone started singing the college song, and he sang too, loudly. Swati squeezed his arm.

qa.q: What did the poster say?
qa.a: FAIR FEES FOR ALL.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling at the gate?
qa.a: Nervous, with shaking hands, and then proud and part of something when he sang with everyone.

qa.q: How did Harish weigh the risks before going?
qa.a: He thought about his exam and his father, checked that the march was peaceful and permitted, and limited himself to one hour.

qa.q: What was it like for Swati to have Harish join?
qa.a: She seemed glad and supportive, squeezing his arm, since the fee hike hit him hardest.

grounding: A student joins a peaceful protest, feeling fear, pride and solidarity, after weighing exams and family worries.

passage: I'd never been to a protest before that night. After a student was harassed near the campus bus stop and the administration did nothing for two weeks, my friend Chandrika said, 'I'm going. You?' My stomach knotted. My parents were in Nagpur and would panic if they saw me on the news. I had lab reports due. But I also thought about walking to that bus stop alone every evening. So I texted Amma where I'd be, and went. Five hundred of us walked from the library to the admin block, holding up phone torches, completely silent. I was scared the whole time, and proud, and part of something enormous. The next week the college put up lights and a guard at the bus stop. I'm Charu. I still get goosebumps.

qa.q: How many students walked from the library to the admin block?
qa.a: Five hundred.

qa.q: How did Charu feel during the march?
qa.a: Scared the whole time, but also proud and part of something enormous.

qa.q: What did Charu do to reduce the risk before going?
qa.a: Texted Amma the plan and joined a silent, peaceful march with a friend.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt when Charu came along?
qa.a: Probably relieved and encouraged, glad not to go alone.

grounding: A young adult joins a peaceful campus march out of conviction, feeling fear, pride and solidarity together.

passage: Faculty mentor's note, Thursday. Sharmila, from my second-year group, came to see me before today's march for the farm workers' wage campaign. She wanted to go but was scared: her scholarship depends on attendance, and her uncle had warned her about 'getting a record'. We talked it through. I told her the march had police permission and a fixed route, and that attendance would be excused for registered participants. She decided to go for two hours with her friend Santosh, stay near the front marshals and leave before dark. She came back at six, sunburnt and shaking a little. 'I was terrified, and I've never felt so proud,' she said. I have asked the department to share the excused-attendance rule with all students.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila worried about her scholarship?
qa.a: It depends on attendance.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel after the march?
qa.a: Terrified and also prouder than ever, sunburnt and a little shaky.

qa.q: How did Sharmila weigh the risk before joining?
qa.a: She talked with her mentor, checked the march had permission and excused attendance, and planned to go with Santosh for two hours near the marshals and leave before dark.

qa.q: What might Santosh's company have meant to Sharmila?
qa.a: Having a friend beside her likely made her feel safer and less alone during the march.

grounding: A mentor's note on a student who weighs risks to studies and family before joining a peaceful march, and feels fear and pride.

passage: When Uma came home to Dharwad district for the holidays, the whole village knew she had been leading the students' protest for clean drinking water at the tehsil office. Her mother, Sarita, didn't sleep the first night. At breakfast she finally said, 'People are talking. What if the police take you? Who will marry a girl who shouts on the road?' Uma's first instinct was to snap, 'I'm not a child.' Instead she put down her roti. 'Amma, tell me what scares you most.' Sarita talked for twenty minutes: about a cousin who was once arrested, about the neighbours. Uma listened, then explained how the protests were organised: permission letters, women volunteers, no violence. 'Will you tell me before each one?' Sarita asked. 'Every time,' Uma said.

qa.q: What was the student protest for?
qa.a: Clean drinking water, at the tehsil office.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when her mother first raised her fears?
qa.a: Uma felt a flash of defensive frustration, wanting to snap 'I'm not a child', but chose calm instead.

qa.q: What did Uma do instead of arguing?
qa.a: She asked what scared her mother most, listened for twenty minutes, then calmly explained how the protests are organised.

qa.q: What is Sarita most afraid of?
qa.a: Uma's safety, remembering a cousin who was arrested, and the family's reputation and Uma's marriage prospects.

grounding: A young woman's mother fears for her safety and reputation over her activism, and calm conversation helps more than defiance.

passage: Anders had been out every Friday with the climate group outside Stockholm's city hall, holding a banner with forty other students. His mother, Selin, found out from a neighbour's photo. That evening she was waiting in the kitchen, arms folded. 'Do you know what happens to people who get arrested? No job, no future!' Anders felt the old anger rise. He wanted to slam the door, as he had at sixteen. Instead he sat down. 'Mamma, what exactly are you scared of?' Selin's voice shook. She talked about her brother in Izmir, arrested at a protest years ago, who lost his teaching job. Anders hadn't known. He showed her the group's rules: permits, no blocking roads, trained stewards. She was still worried. But she asked if she could come along one Friday and see.

qa.q: Where did the climate group stand every Friday?
qa.a: Outside Stockholm's city hall.

qa.q: What did Anders feel when his mother confronted him?
qa.a: The old anger rising and an urge to slam the door, as at sixteen, before he chose to sit down.

qa.q: What turned the argument into a calmer conversation?
qa.a: Anders asking what exactly she feared, listening to her brother's story, then showing her the group's safety rules.

qa.q: Why is Selin so afraid of Anders's activism?
qa.a: Her brother in Izmir was arrested at a protest and lost his teaching job, so her fear is about Anders's safety and future.

grounding: A young man's mother is frightened by his activism, and calm talk about risk helps more than defiance.

passage: The college counsellor's room was too small for four people and one big worry. Harsha sat between her parents; Ms Sarika Nair, the counsellor, sat across from them. 'We saw Harsha's face on the news, at the march about hostel curfews,' her father said. 'People from our community called. What if she's expelled? What will relatives say?' Harsha opened her mouth to argue, then caught Ms Nair's eye. Ms Nair asked, 'What would help you feel less afraid?' Her mother said quietly, 'Knowing where she is. Knowing it's peaceful.' Harsha nodded. 'I can tell you before every march. And I won't go to any that isn't approved.' Her father let out a long breath. 'And your studies?' 'Top three in the class,' Harsha said. Her mother almost smiled.

qa.q: What was the march about?
qa.a: Hostel curfews.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel when her father listed his fears?
qa.a: Harsha felt a defensive urge to argue, then chose calm after catching Ms Nair's eye.

qa.q: How did Ms Nair help the family?
qa.a: She asked the parents what would make them less afraid, which turned blame into specific needs Harsha could meet.

qa.q: What were Harsha's parents most afraid of?
qa.a: Harsha's safety and possible expulsion, and what the community and relatives would say.

grounding: A student's parents fear for her safety and reputation over activism, and a calm, guided conversation about risk helps.
